subject.title: Choriambics
subject.author: Algernon Charles Swinburne
subject.text:
Love, what ailed thee to leave life that was made lovely, we thought, with love?
What sweet visions of sleep lured thee away, down from the light above?

What strange faces of dreams, voices that called, hands that were raised to wave,
Lured or led thee, alas, out of the sun, down to the sunless grave?

Ah, thy luminous eyes! once was their light fed with the fire of day;
Now their shadowy lids cover them close, hush them and hide away.

Ah, thy snow-coloured hands! once were they chains, mighty to bind me fast;
Now no blood in them burns, mindless of love, senseless of passion past.

Ah, thy beautiful hair! so was it once braided for me, for me;
Now for death is it crowned, only for death, lover and lord of thee.

Sweet, the kisses of death set on thy lips, colder are they than mine;
Colder surely than past kisses that love poured for thy lips as wine.

Lov'st thou death? is his face fairer than love's, brighter to look upon?
Seest thou light in his eyes, light by which love's pales and is overshone?

Lo the roses of death, grey as the dust, chiller of leaf than snow!
Why let fall from thy hand love's that were thine, roses that loved thee so?

Large red lilies of love, sceptral and tall, lovely for eyes to see;
Thornless blossom of love, full of the sun, fruits that were reared for thee.

Now death's poppies alone circle thy hair, girdle thy breasts as white;
Bloodless blossoms of death, leaves that have sprung never against the light.

Nay then, sleep if thou wilt; love is content; what should he do to weep?
Sweet was love to thee once; now in thine eyes sweeter than love is sleep.

title: The One Metre Built to Tell You to Let Go — and Doesn't
standfirst: Only two Latin poems in this exact rhythm survive complete, and both are telling someone to move on — from grief, or from a broken friendship. When Swinburne borrowed the shape for English, he kept the metre and threw out the instruction.

sections.heading: Sixteen Syllables, Twenty-Two Lines, No Exceptions
sections.body: A choriamb is one borrowed shape: long-short-short-long, a trochee welded to an iamb, a foot the record credits to the little-known third-century-BC poet Asclepiades of Samos, according to [Edmund Gosse's 1911 entry](https://en.wikisource.org/wiki/1911_Encyclop%C3%A6dia_Britannica/Choriambic_Verse) on choriambic verse for the Encyclopaedia Britannica. Stack three of those feet between two free opening syllables and a closing iamb, and the result is the line Swinburne is using here: what classicists call the greater Asclepiad, sixteen syllables in a fixed order — two syllables, choriamb, choriamb, choriamb, iamb — never varied. Count the poem's own opening line against that template: *Love, what ailed thee to leave life that was made lovely, we thought, with love?* comes out to exactly sixteen syllables. So does every other line. Twenty-two lines, eleven rhymed couplets, the same borrowed shape without a single departure. The rhyme is Swinburne's own addition. Horace and Catullus wrote this metre quantitative and unrhymed, since Latin verse did not rhyme at all; Swinburne's couplets do — love/above, wave/grave, day/away — an English ornament bolted onto a skeleton that never carried one in antiquity.

sections.heading: The Only Two Latin Poems Built the Same Way
sections.body: In Greek lyric the greater Asclepiad was common property — Sappho, Alcaeus, Callimachus and Theocritus are all named as users of it in the same Britannica entry. In Latin it survives far more rarely: among complete poems, only Horace's Odes 1.11 and 4.10 and Catullus's poem 30 use the unmixed form (Horace also folds it into a mixed stanza in Ode 1.18), according to Wikipedia's account of the Asclepiad metres. Both of the subjects that do survive whole are instructions to stop dwelling on something. Horace's Ode 1.11 tells a woman named Leuconoe not to ask how much time she has left and not to trust tomorrow; its last stanza supplies the phrase every schoolchild mangles, [carpe diem](https://classicalstudies.support/about/the-latin-page/horace-odes-1-11/) — pluck the day, rather than seize it, since the verb is about harvesting, not violence. Catullus's poem opens *Alfene immemor atque unanimis false sodalibus* — forgetful Alfenus, false to united comrades, in the [Latin text given](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Catullus_30) on Wikipedia — and spends its remaining lines telling a friend to stop pretending a betrayal never happened. Stop waiting for death; stop pretending nothing broke. That is what this metre says, in both poems that survive whole from Rome. Swinburne picks up the same sixteen syllables and does neither.

sections.heading: A Brave Attempt, According to the Man Who Praised It
sections.body: Edmund Gosse was a friend of Swinburne's for decades and later his biographer, and it was Gosse who summed up this experiment for the public record, in an entry on choriambic verse he wrote for the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. After tracing the metre through Sappho, Alcaeus and Horace, Gosse turns to [his own friend's poem](https://en.wikisource.org/wiki/1911_Encyclop%C3%A6dia_Britannica/Choriambic_Verse) and writes that "Swinburne even introduced it into English poetry," quoting this poem's opening lines as his example and judging the result "a brave attempt to resuscitate the measured sound of the greater asclepiad." Read that twice and the compliment gets smaller. An attempt is not a success, and brave is the word reserved for efforts that do not quite land as often as for the ones that do. Gosse never claims the metre became usable in English — only that his friend tried it with some courage. He was not wrong to hedge: outside this one poem, almost nothing in the following decades picked up the greater Asclepiad in English at all.

sections.heading: The One Poet Who Tried It Again
sections.body: Thirty years later, a Cambridge undergraduate tried the same borrowed shape twice, and filed both results under "Experiments" rather than finished work. Rupert Brooke's "Choriambics — I" and "Choriambics — II" sit in that section of [his collected poems](https://www.gutenberg.org/cache/epub/262/pg262-images.html), written between 1908 and 1911 according to the same volume's own table of contents. "Choriambics — I" opens *Ah! not now, when desire burns, and the wind calls, and the suns of spring* — a speaker refusing a woman's comfort not because of death but because he still has songs to sing and fights to fight, and promising to want her voice only once life is over. "Choriambics — II" opens *Here the flame that was ash, shrine that was void, lost in the haunted wood*, and describes a devotee tending an empty shrine for a god who turns out, by the poem's end, to already be dead on foreign soil. Both poems were gathered into The Collected Poems of Rupert Brooke, with an introduction by George Edward Woodberry and a biographical note by Margaret Lavington, in [an edition dated 1915](https://theotherpages.org/poems/books/brooke/brooke04.html) — the same year Brooke himself died of septicaemia aboard a French hospital ship moored off the Greek island of Skyros, as [Wikipedia records](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rupert_Brooke). Nothing ties those dates together on purpose. It remains true that the only other substantial English use of this exact Roman shape, before the war that killed its author, chose to run the same current as Swinburne's: love losing out to death.

sections.heading: A Refusal to Move On, Published a Year Before a Rescue
sections.body: Poems and Ballads: Second Series, the volume that carries "Choriambics," appeared in 1878, a collection that Wikipedia's account of the book describes as less political than Swinburne's earlier work and markedly shaped by French literature — poems to Baudelaire, Gautier, Hugo and Théodore de Banville sit alongside it. Fourteen months later, in September 1879, the critic Theodore Watts-Dunton moved a 42-year-old Swinburne, by then collapsing under years of heavy drinking, into [his own house at Putney](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Algernon_Charles_Swinburne) and kept him there, sober and cared for, for the rest of his life. The verdict on what that rescue did to the poetry, recorded on the same page, is blunt: "It was said of Watts-Dunton that he saved the man and killed the poet." No source consulted here names a real person "Choriambics" mourns, and it would be dishonest to invent one where the record stays quiet; Swinburne wrote plenty of elegies for no one in particular. What the poem does insist on, in its own last line, is that sleep has become dearer than love ever was — its final words are "sweeter than love is sleep" — a refusal to be talked out of grief that sits strangely close to a poet about to be rescued from himself whether he agreed to it or not. He got thirty more years at the Pines. Whatever "Choriambics" is mourning, it does not want them.
